screens.title: Understanding Unreal Engine's Object Model and Garbage Collection
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why Unreal's UObject-based object model matters for every C++ system you write in the engine. UObject is not just a base class; it provides reflection, serialization, networking hooks, editor integration, and a custom garbage collector that controls lifetime. You'll see how macros like UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION feed into a generated runtime description via the Unreal Header Tool, and why those generated descriptions matter for editor visibility and for the garbage collector to see references. We'll also cover the correct way to create UObjects with NewObject (), how the Outer relationship influences ownership, and common pitfalls such as using raw new or unmarked UObject pointers that lead to dangling references. A practical example walks through making a simple UMyDataContainer, adding a tracked UPROPERTY to an actor, and instantiating it safely in BeginPlay. By the end you'll be able to explain why marking UObject pointers and using NewObject () prevents crashes and lost objects, and you'll have a clear troubleshooting checklist for pointer safety. Consider how forgetting UPROPERTY could silently cause a crash in a shipped level: that's the practical risk you will learn to avoid.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Understanding UObject & GC
Understanding UObject & Garbage Collection
Why UObject, reflection, and NewObject matter for safe C++ in Unreal Engine

Unreal's UObject system centralizes features that raw C++ does not offer. It enables runtime reflection, serialization, networking, editor integration, and a garbage collector that only sees references declared via the reflection system. Learning these relationships prevents crashes and makes your components interoperable with the engine and editor.

Reflection
UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION feed UHT for runtime metadata.
GC
Engine GC traverses objects starting from root set to find reachable UObjects.
New Objects
Use NewObject<T> with an Outer to register with the engine.
Explore Key Topics
UObject Essentials
Why classes derive from UObject and what they gain.
Reflection & UHT
How macros become generated metadata the engine uses.
Garbage Collection
Reachability from root objects determines object lifetime.
Concept Map
A compact view tying reflection, object creation, and GC together. Use this mental model while you code and when debugging lifetime problems.
Reflection flow
UCLASS/UPROPERTY → UHT → .generated.h → runtime metadata
GC flow
Root objects → reachability traversal → collect unreachable UObjects
Quick example
Create a UMyDataContainer derived from UObject, add a UPROPERTY int, instantiate it with NewObject in an Actor's BeginPlay, then log the value to verify correct creation and GC tracking.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll build practical skills for safely using Unreal's UObject system. First, you'll explain why UObject is the backbone of most engine features and how it differs from plain C++ objects. Second, you'll describe the reflection system and how UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION produce metadata the engine uses at runtime. Third, you'll understand Unreal's garbage collection: roots, reachability, and how the GC decides which objects to reclaim. Finally, you'll learn correct code patterns: using UPROPERTY to mark UObject pointers, constructing instances with NewObject (), and choosing weak or shared pointers when appropriate for non-owning or non-UObject types. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can check your understanding by inspecting real code and confirming the engine shows your properties in the editor or logs your created object's activity. These are practical, not theoretical goals: being able to mark, create, and diagnose UObject lifetimes prevents subtle runtime crashes in your projects.

screens.title: What is UObject and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: UObject is the foundational engine object that provides features beyond regular C++ objects. As a definition, a UObject-derived class participates in Unreal's reflection and runtime systems, which gives it serialization, editor exposure, networking replication hooks, and garbage collection integration. Practically, this means classes that need to be visible to the editor or to the engine's runtime systems should derive from UObject so the engine can manage them properly. A concrete example is a UActorComponent or UDataAsset: both inherit UObject and therefore are serialized, can expose properties to designers, and are tracked by GC. A common misconception is to treat UObject like a plain struct or a stack-allocated helper type; while you can write plain C++ helpers, any object that you want the engine to save, show in the editor, or manage across the world lifecycle must be a UObject. Another confusion is thinking UObject replaces standard C++ resource management — it complements it: non-UObject data still needs standard smart pointers or manual deletion. Key takeaway: use UObject for engine-managed objects so the engine can participate in construction, destruction, and lifetime decisions on your behalf. How might a gameplay system behave incorrectly if its core data type is not a UObject and therefore invisible to the editor and GC?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: UObject is the engine-managed base class that enables reflection, serialization, editor integration, networking, and GC for derived objects.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is UObject
UObject — core definition
Engine-managed base that provides reflection and GC integration.
  • Reflection: The engine knows about properties and functions at runtime.
  • Serialization: Save and load object state to disk.
  • Garbage Collection: The engine can track and reclaim UObjects automatically.
Common misconception
Assuming UObject behaves like a non-managed C++ type leads to missing GC tracking, lost editor exposure, and subtle crashes.
Concrete example
UActorComponent and UDataAsset both derive from UObject. Because of that inheritance, their properties are serialized, the editor can show them, and the GC can keep them alive while referenced. If you instead store component data in a raw C++ class, the engine will not automatically save or manage it.
Key Takeaway
Derive from UObject when you need engine-level features; otherwise use plain C++ with explicit memory management.

screens.title: Reflection system: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION, and UHT
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's reflection system lets the engine inspect classes, properties, and functions at runtime. When you annotate code with UCLASS, UPROPERTY, or UFUNCTION, the Unreal Header Tool parses your headers and generates additional C++ code that builds a runtime description of those elements. That generated code is how the editor displays property fields, how Blueprints can call C++ functions, and how the garbage collector discovers references. A concrete example: declaring UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) on a float not only allows designers to edit the value, it tells UHT to emit metadata describing the property's type and attributes so the engine can serialize and display it appropriately. A common misconception is that the macros themselves perform reflection at compile time; in reality, they are markers that UHT uses to generate supporting code. A failure to use these macros when needed results in properties that are invisible to the editor and invisible to GC tracking. Key takeaway: when a member must be seen by the engine or tracked by GC, annotate it and rely on UHT-generated code to make it discoverable at runtime. Reflection system: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION, and UHT means uclass/uproperty/ufunction are markers processed by uht to emit generated code that provides runtime metadata and engine visibility.. In practical terms, how macros become runtime metadata through code generation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reflection summary
keyIdea.text: UCLASS/UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION are markers processed by UHT to emit generated code that provides runtime metadata and engine visibility.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Reflection System
How the reflection pipeline works
  1. Annotate headers with UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION.
  2. UHT parses these markers and generates additional header/source code into .generated.h files.
  3. The generated code builds runtime metadata used by the editor, Blueprints, and GC.
Concrete example
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) float MyValue tells UHT about the property type and editor attributes so the engine can display and serialize it.
Common mistakes & checks
  • Forgetting UPROPERTY means the GC and editor will not see the field.
  • Assume macros are processed by UHT; check generated headers to confirm expected metadata exists.
  • Use UFUNCTION when you need Blueprint accessibility or RPC hooks.
Why this matters
Generated reflection data is the bridge between your C++ and the engine features that rely on runtime awareness.

screens.title: How UPROPERTY affects GC tracking
screens.narratorSegment: A critical rule in Unreal C++ is that any UObject* pointer that should keep an object alive must be marked with UPROPERTY. If a UObject member is decorated with UPROPERTY, the reflection system will include that reference in the engine's object graph, which the garbage collector traverses to determine reachability. A concrete contrast: a UStaticMeshComponent* decorated with UPROPERTY will be seen by GC and kept alive while referenced; the same pointer without UPROPERTY is invisible to GC and becomes a dangling pointer if the pointed object is collected. A common misconception is that a raw pointer is fine as long as you manually set it; in practice, the engine's GC can collect objects unexpectedly if it cannot see the reference. Example snippet in the chapter highlights both cases conceptually. To avoid mistakes, prefer UPROPERTY for member pointers, or use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning links where you explicitly accept the object can be collected and you will check validity before use. Key takeaway: UPROPERTY is not cosmetic — it determines whether the engine tracks the reference or not. How would your gameplay behave if a vital component pointer were not tracked by GC?

keyIdea.title: Tracking rule
keyIdea.text: Mark UObject member pointers with UPROPERTY to ensure the garbage collector recognizes and preserves those references.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › UPROPERTY & GC
Correct (GC-tracked)
UPROPERTY() on a UObject* member registers the reference in the reflection data so GC will consider the referenced object reachable.
Behavior
Object remains alive while referenced by UPROPERTY members during GC passes.
Incorrect (not tracked)
A raw UObject* without UPROPERTY is invisible to the generated reflection data and thus invisible to GC traversal, risking premature collection and dangling pointers.
Risk
Crash or undefined behavior when GC reclaims the referenced object.
Guidelines
  • Use UPROPERTY for owning member pointers to UObjects.
  • Use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references and check IsValid before use.
  • When in doubt, mark the member with UPROPERTY and document ownership semantics.

screens.title: Garbage collection mechanics for UObjects
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's garbage collection for UObjects is based on reachability from a set of root objects. Root objects include engine-level singletons like the game instance and world objects, and anything explicitly added to the root set. During a GC pass, the engine traverses the object graph using the references known through reflection data. Any UObject reachable from a root is considered referenced and will not be collected. Objects that are not reachable become eligible for reclamation. A concrete example: if an actor holds a UPROPERTY pointer to a data object, the data object remains reachable while the actor is alive; when the actor is destroyed and no other references exist, the data object becomes collectible. A common misconception is to equate UE GC with tracing systems that immediately finalize objects; UE's GC behavior depends on the timing of GC passes and on whether references are recorded in the reflection system. If you need guaranteed lifetime beyond reachability, AddToRoot can keep an object alive, but this should be used sparingly. Key takeaway: design ownership and reference graphs so essential objects remain reachable from known roots, and use weak pointers where you intentionally accept ephemeral links. How would you reorganize ownership to avoid dangling references in your current project?

keyIdea.title: GC flow
keyIdea.text: GC marks UObjects reachable from roots during traversal; unreferenced objects are reclaimed during collection passes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Garbage Collection
Garbage collection process
1. Roots
UGameInstance, UWorld, or objects added with AddToRoot act as traversal starting points.
2. Traversal
Engine follows references recorded by reflection data to mark reachable objects.
3. Collection
Objects not marked as reachable are eligible for reclamation in the GC pass.
Practical note: GC timing and how often passes run can affect when an unreachable object is reclaimed. For predictable lifetimes, maintain clear ownership hierarchies, use UPROPERTY for strong references, and prefer weak pointers when you accept collection may happen.
Example scenario
An actor creates a UMyDataContainer with NewObject and stores it in a UPROPERTY member. While actor exists, data container is reachable. When actor is destroyed and no other references exist, the container becomes collectible.
Misconception check
The engine will not track raw pointers for you. If you rely on raw pointers, you may see objects collected unexpectedly during a GC pass.

screens.title: Creating UObjects correctly with NewObject<T>() and Outer
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a UObject must go through the engine's construction path so the object is registered, initialized, and placed in the object hierarchy. NewObject () is the designated factory function; it ensures proper initialization and assigns an Outer, which establishes ownership and often ties lifetime to a containing object. For example, calling NewObject of a data container with the owning actor as the Outer registers the container under that actor's hierarchy so if the actor is destroyed, the container's reachability will reflect that relationship. A common mistake is to use new directly for UObject-derived classes which bypasses engine registration, leaving objects untracked by garbage collection and the editor. Another practical point: pass an appropriate Outer—often this is the actor or component that logically owns the new object. If no clear owner exists, consider a longer-lived Outer such as the world or game instance, but be careful: choosing an overly long-lived Outer can prevent expected collection. Key takeaway: always use NewObject () and set the correct Outer when you want the engine to manage the object's lifecycle properly. How would you pick an Outer for a temporary helper object versus a designer asset?

keyIdea.title: Creation rule
keyIdea.text: Use NewObject<T>(Outer) to construct UObjects so they are registered, initialized, and placed in the engine ownership hierarchy.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › NewObject & Outer
NewObject instantiation
NewObject ensures the engine registers the UObject and assigns an Outer which participates in lifetime and hierarchy.
Example usage (conceptual)
// Create an instance with the owning actor as Outer
// NewObject<UMyCustomObject>(OwnerActor);
The exact code above registers the object with the engine and places it under OwnerActor's hierarchy for GC purposes.
Guidelines for choosing an Outer
  • Choose the logical owner: an actor for actor-owned data, a component for component-owned resources.
  • For global resources, a long-lived Outer such as GameInstance may be appropriate, but avoid leaking objects by over-long ownership.
  • Avoid raw new; it bypasses engine registration and GC tracking.
Key takeaway
NewObject is the safe factory and Outer defines the ownership path for GC and hierarchy.

screens.title: Hands-on example: UMyDataContainer and using it in an Actor
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical example that ties reflection, creation, and GC together. First you create UMyDataContainer derived from UObject. In the header you add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 MyIntValue and a UFUNCTION to expose behavior. This tells the engine about the property and function so they appear in editor or Blueprint systems. In the implementation, PrintMyData logs the property's value using the engine logging and on-screen debug facilities. Then, inside an actor's BeginPlay you create the container with NewObject and pass the actor as Outer so the object is owned and tracked by that actor. A misconception to avoid: do not call new to allocate the data container. That bypasses engine registration and makes the container invisible to GC. The concrete run-through in the chapter shows how instantiating the container and calling PrintMyData produces on-screen messages proving correct creation and lifetime. Key takeaway: this sequence — declare with macros, implement behavior, instantiate with NewObject and set the Outer — is the standard, safe way to use UObjects in gameplay code. How would you extend this pattern to support saving and loading the container's state?

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › UMyDataContainer Walkthrough
Header: UMyDataContainer (concept)
// UMyDataContainer.h (excerpt)
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/NoExportTypes.h"
#include "MyDataContainer.generated.h"

UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType)
class MYFIRSTCPPPROJECT_API UMyDataContainer : public UObject
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Data")
  int32 MyIntValue;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Data")
  void PrintMyData();
};
Implementation & usage
// UMyDataContainer.cpp (excerpt)
#include "MyDataContainer.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h"

void UMyDataContainer::PrintMyData()
{
  if (GEngine)
  {
    GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Magenta,
      FString::Printf(TEXT("MyDataContainer's Int Value: %d"), MyIntValue));
  }
}

// In an actor's BeginPlay:
// MyDataInstance = NewObject(this);
// MyDataInstance->MyIntValue = 42;
// MyDataInstance->PrintMyData();
Observe the log or on-screen message to confirm correct creation and GC-aware ownership via the actor Outer.

screens.title: Common memory pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: This screen lists the most common memory mistakes in Unreal C++ and how to mitigate them. First, dangling pointers arise when you hold a raw UObject* pointer without UPROPERTY and the referenced object is garbage collected; always use UPROPERTY for member pointers that represent ownership. Second, using new to instantiate UObject-derived classes bypasses engine registration and the GC; prefer NewObject () for proper initialization and tracking. Fourth, mixing raw C++ smart pointers with UObject lifetimes is a mismatch: use TSharedPtr or TUniquePtr only for pure C++ types, not for UObjects. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Common Pitfalls
Common mistakes
  • Dangling pointers: Raw UObject* without UPROPERTY may be collected, leading to crashes. Remedy: use UPROPERTY.
  • Using new: new bypasses engine registration. Remedy: NewObject<T>.
  • Circular references: Mutual UPROPERTY references can complicate GC. Remedy: use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning links.
  • Pointer type mismatch: Use TSharedPtr/TUniquePtr for non-UObject C++ types only.
Mitigation steps
  1. Audit members: mark UObject* with UPROPERTY when ownership is needed.
  2. Replace new allocations of UObjects with NewObject and a sensible Outer.
  3. Use weak pointers for non-owning references and validate before use.
  4. Log lifecycle events to confirm when objects are created and destroyed.
Key takeaway
Match pointer and ownership models and prefer engine-approved patterns to prevent hard-to-debug failures.

screens.title: Collections and container safety with TArray and UPROPERTY
screens.narratorSegment: When managing collections of UObjects, the safe pattern is to use engine-aware containers combined with reflection annotations. For example, a TArray of UObject pointers stored as a UPROPERTY will be included in reflection data so the garbage collector can follow contained references during traversal. This means a UPROPERTY TArray<UMyObject*> keeps each object reachable while the array itself remains reachable. If the TArray is not a UPROPERTY, the GC may not inspect its contents and those UObjects could be collected incorrectly. Practical example: a component managing a list of dynamically created helper objects should declare the container as UPROPERTY to ensure lifetime is tied to the owner. A common mistake is to keep a non-UPROPERTY TArray of UObject pointers; that pattern silently defeats GC tracking. For non-UObject containers or pure value types, standard C++ containers and smart pointers are still appropriate. Key takeaway: mark any container that holds UObject pointers with UPROPERTY so the engine can traverse and preserve the referenced objects. When you audit a class, check both the container and its element types for proper annotation. screens.title: Debugging UObject lifetime issues and testing patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When you suspect a UObject lifecycle issue, follow reproducible debugging steps. First, add explicit nullptr checks and use IsValid or TWeakObjectPtr checks before dereferencing to prevent crashes. Second, add logging and on-screen messages at creation and destruction points to observe when objects are spawned and when they disappear. Third, create small controlled tests: instantiate the object with NewObject in BeginPlay, then remove references and force a GC pass if your build supports it to observe behavior. A common misconception is that removing a single pointer is enough to guarantee collection; because GC depends on reachability from root objects and the timing of GC passes, you must understand what else may reference your object. If you need to prevent collection for debug, temporarily AddToRoot but remember to RemoveFromRoot to avoid leaks. Key takeaway: use defensive checks and controlled experiments to locate missing UPROPERTYs or incorrect Outers. What minimal repro would you create to demonstrate a missing UPROPERTY causing a crash? Steps to reproduce lifecycle issues
1. Add logs when objects are created and right before they are expected to be destroyed. Observe timestamps and context.
2. Use IsValid or TWeakObjectPtr checks before using pointers to avoid crashes while investigating.
3. Build a minimal repro: create the object in BeginPlay, clear references, and run to see if GC reclaims it unexpectedly.
Pro tip
Temporarily add logging for the object's address and Outer to inspect ownership at runtime.
Quick check list
  • Is the pointer a UPROPERTY or TWeakObjectPtr?
  • Was the object created with NewObject and given the expected Outer?
  • Are there unexpected references preventing collection or missing references causing premature collection?

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts will help you reason about object lifetime and engine integration. First, UObject is the engine-managed base class that enables reflection, serialization, editor exposure, and garbage collection; use it when your object must interact with engine systems. Second, the reflection macros UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION are markers processed by the Unreal Header Tool, which generates metadata the engine uses for editor visibility, Blueprints, and GC tracking. Third, memory safety depends on following engine patterns: create UObjects with NewObject and mark owning pointers with UPROPERTY; use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references and C++ smart pointers only for non-UObject data. Keep these principles in mind when you design ownership across actors, components, and assets so that objects remain reachable when needed and are collectible when not. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why Unreal's UObject-based object model matters for every C++ system you write in the engine. UObject is not just a base class; it provides reflection, serialization, networking hooks, editor integration, and a custom garbage collector that controls lifetime. You'll see how macros like UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION feed into a generated runtime description via the Unreal Header Tool, and why those generated descriptions matter for editor visibility and for the garbage collector to see references. We'll also cover the correct way to create UObjects with NewObject (), how the Outer relationship influences ownership, and common pitfalls such as using raw new or unmarked UObject pointers that lead to dangling references. A practical example walks through making a simple UMyDataContainer, adding a tracked UPROPERTY to an actor, and instantiating it safely in BeginPlay. By the end you'll be able to explain why marking UObject pointers and using NewObject () prevents crashes and lost objects, and you'll have a clear troubleshooting checklist for pointer safety. Consider how forgetting UPROPERTY could silently cause a crash in a shipped level: that's the practical risk you will learn to avoid.

Over the next screens you'll build practical skills for safely using Unreal's UObject system. First, you'll explain why UObject is the backbone of most engine features and how it differs from plain C++ objects. Second, you'll describe the reflection system and how UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION produce metadata the engine uses at runtime. Third, you'll understand Unreal's garbage collection: roots, reachability, and how the GC decides which objects to reclaim. Finally, you'll learn correct code patterns: using UPROPERTY to mark UObject pointers, constructing instances with NewObject (), and choosing weak or shared pointers when appropriate for non-owning or non-UObject types. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can check your understanding by inspecting real code and confirming the engine shows your properties in the editor or logs your created object's activity. These are practical, not theoretical goals: being able to mark, create, and diagnose UObject lifetimes prevents subtle runtime crashes in your projects.

These objectives are paired with hands-on checks so you can validate your understanding. For example, after learning what UObject provides, create a minimal UObject-derived class and expose a property; verify that the editor or the generated metadata recognizes that property. After studying reflection, add a UFUNCTION and confirm BlueprintCallable exposure in a test Blueprint. To validate garbage-collected lifetimes, allocate an object with NewObject () inside an Actor's BeginPlay and confirm the object survives as long as the actor does, then remove references and observe collection behavior. Finally, for safe patterns, deliberately replace a UPROPERTY pointer with an unmarked raw pointer and observe the crash risk in a controlled test; then convert it back to UPROPERTY to see stability return. Each of these small experiments proves the learning objective and gives you repeatable steps to follow when auditing unfamiliar code in larger projects.

UObject is the foundational engine object that provides features beyond regular C++ objects. As a definition, a UObject-derived class participates in Unreal's reflection and runtime systems, which gives it serialization, editor exposure, networking replication hooks, and garbage collection integration. Practically, this means classes that need to be visible to the editor or to the engine's runtime systems should derive from UObject so the engine can manage them properly. A concrete example is a UActorComponent or UDataAsset: both inherit UObject and therefore are serialized, can expose properties to designers, and are tracked by GC. A common misconception is to treat UObject like a plain struct or a stack-allocated helper type; while you can write plain C++ helpers, any object that you want the engine to save, show in the editor, or manage across the world lifecycle must be a UObject. Another confusion is thinking UObject replaces standard C++ resource management — it complements it: non-UObject data still needs standard smart pointers or manual deletion. Key takeaway: use UObject for engine-managed objects so the engine can participate in construction, destruction, and lifetime decisions on your behalf. How might a gameplay system behave incorrectly if its core data type is not a UObject and therefore invisible to the editor and GC?

Unreal's reflection system lets the engine inspect classes, properties, and functions at runtime. When you annotate code with UCLASS, UPROPERTY, or UFUNCTION, the Unreal Header Tool parses your headers and generates additional C++ code that builds a runtime description of those elements. That generated code is how the editor displays property fields, how Blueprints can call C++ functions, and how the garbage collector discovers references. A concrete example: declaring UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) on a float not only allows designers to edit the value, it tells UHT to emit metadata describing the property's type and attributes so the engine can serialize and display it appropriately. A common misconception is that the macros themselves perform reflection at compile time; in reality, they are markers that UHT uses to generate supporting code. A failure to use these macros when needed results in properties that are invisible to the editor and invisible to GC tracking. Key takeaway: when a member must be seen by the engine or tracked by GC, annotate it and rely on UHT-generated code to make it discoverable at runtime. Reflection system: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION, and UHT means uclass/uproperty/ufunction are markers processed by uht to emit generated code that provides runtime metadata and engine visibility.. In practical terms, how macros become runtime metadata through code generation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A critical rule in Unreal C++ is that any UObject* pointer that should keep an object alive must be marked with UPROPERTY. If a UObject member is decorated with UPROPERTY, the reflection system will include that reference in the engine's object graph, which the garbage collector traverses to determine reachability. A concrete contrast: a UStaticMeshComponent* decorated with UPROPERTY will be seen by GC and kept alive while referenced; the same pointer without UPROPERTY is invisible to GC and becomes a dangling pointer if the pointed object is collected. A common misconception is that a raw pointer is fine as long as you manually set it; in practice, the engine's GC can collect objects unexpectedly if it cannot see the reference. Example snippet in the chapter highlights both cases conceptually. To avoid mistakes, prefer UPROPERTY for member pointers, or use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning links where you explicitly accept the object can be collected and you will check validity before use. Key takeaway: UPROPERTY is not cosmetic — it determines whether the engine tracks the reference or not. How would your gameplay behave if a vital component pointer were not tracked by GC?

Unreal's garbage collection for UObjects is based on reachability from a set of root objects. Root objects include engine-level singletons like the game instance and world objects, and anything explicitly added to the root set. During a GC pass, the engine traverses the object graph using the references known through reflection data. Any UObject reachable from a root is considered referenced and will not be collected. Objects that are not reachable become eligible for reclamation. A concrete example: if an actor holds a UPROPERTY pointer to a data object, the data object remains reachable while the actor is alive; when the actor is destroyed and no other references exist, the data object becomes collectible. A common misconception is to equate UE GC with tracing systems that immediately finalize objects; UE's GC behavior depends on the timing of GC passes and on whether references are recorded in the reflection system. If you need guaranteed lifetime beyond reachability, AddToRoot can keep an object alive, but this should be used sparingly. Key takeaway: design ownership and reference graphs so essential objects remain reachable from known roots, and use weak pointers where you intentionally accept ephemeral links. How would you reorganize ownership to avoid dangling references in your current project?

Creating a UObject must go through the engine's construction path so the object is registered, initialized, and placed in the object hierarchy. NewObject () is the designated factory function; it ensures proper initialization and assigns an Outer, which establishes ownership and often ties lifetime to a containing object. For example, calling NewObject of a data container with the owning actor as the Outer registers the container under that actor's hierarchy so if the actor is destroyed, the container's reachability will reflect that relationship. A common mistake is to use new directly for UObject-derived classes which bypasses engine registration, leaving objects untracked by garbage collection and the editor. Another practical point: pass an appropriate Outer—often this is the actor or component that logically owns the new object. If no clear owner exists, consider a longer-lived Outer such as the world or game instance, but be careful: choosing an overly long-lived Outer can prevent expected collection. Key takeaway: always use NewObject () and set the correct Outer when you want the engine to manage the object's lifecycle properly. How would you pick an Outer for a temporary helper object versus a designer asset?

Let's walk through a practical example that ties reflection, creation, and GC together. First you create UMyDataContainer derived from UObject. In the header you add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 MyIntValue and a UFUNCTION to expose behavior. This tells the engine about the property and function so they appear in editor or Blueprint systems. In the implementation, PrintMyData logs the property's value using the engine logging and on-screen debug facilities. Then, inside an actor's BeginPlay you create the container with NewObject and pass the actor as Outer so the object is owned and tracked by that actor. A misconception to avoid: do not call new to allocate the data container. That bypasses engine registration and makes the container invisible to GC. The concrete run-through in the chapter shows how instantiating the container and calling PrintMyData produces on-screen messages proving correct creation and lifetime. Key takeaway: this sequence — declare with macros, implement behavior, instantiate with NewObject and set the Outer — is the standard, safe way to use UObjects in gameplay code. How would you extend this pattern to support saving and loading the container's state?
